messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had always been a private person, but after the stalking incident, he became consumed by an unshakeable sense that the world was a perilous place. It started with small things – constantly looking over his shoulder on the bus ride to work, avoiding certain streets at night, and being extra cautious when meeting new people online for freelance UX design projects. As time passed, this hypervigilance seeped into every aspect of his life. He found himself wondering if he was being watched even in the safety of his own apartment, and the mere sound of footsteps outside his door made him jump. The incident itself still felt like a blur. Kofi had met someone on a dating app, and what initially seemed like a harmless connection quickly escalated into an obsession. The person would show up at his workplace, send him endless messages, and even appear at his favorite coffee shop. Kofi tried to brush it off as an overzealous admirer, but deep down, he knew something was seriously wrong. When the stalker finally disappeared, Kofi was left with a lingering sense of guilt – if only he had been more careful, more discerning, maybe this wouldn't have happened. As a UX designer, Kofi's work required him to be attuned to human behavior and psychological patterns. But now, his professional curiosity felt tainted by an insatiable need for self-protection. He started to see potential threats everywhere – in the way people interacted with each other online, in the design of public spaces, even in the algorithms that governed social media platforms. His once-thriving freelance business began to suffer as he became increasingly withdrawn, turning down projects and avoiding networking events. Kofi's friends and family grew concerned about his growing isolation, but he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was just one misstep away from disaster. He started to doubt his own judgment, wondering if he had inadvertently invited this kind of attention into his life. His usual optimism was replaced by a nagging sense of self-doubt – maybe he wasn't as careful, as aware, or as in control as he thought. As the months went by, Kofi's world shrunk further and further. He stopped attending design meetups, quit his favorite hobby (photography), and even avoided social gatherings with close friends. It was as if he had lost faith in his own ability to navigate the world safely. His online presence, once a source of creative expression, became a liability – every post, every comment, felt like an invitation for potential predators. Kofi's decision to seek help came when he realized that his fear had become all-consuming. He couldn't bear the thought of living in this state of constant vigilance forever, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. As he sat in his dimly lit apartment, surrounded by the familiar comforts of his design work, Kofi finally acknowledged that something needed to change – not just his environment, but his own perception of himself and the world around him.
